# Marketing Strategy Seminar {#sec-marketing-strategy-seminar}

*Marketing strategy* is the central construct of the broader field of strategic
marketing. Where strategic marketing names the field of study, marketing strategy
names its object: the integrated pattern of choices through which a firm creates,
communicates, and delivers value to customers and, by doing so, attains its
objectives. This chapter is a graduate seminar in that construct. It is organized
not as a march through tactics but as a tour of the questions a doctoral student
must be able to pose and answer: what *is* a marketing strategy, how do scholars
build theory about it, how is marketing organized inside the firm to execute it,
and how do the markets the firm serves—customers, channels, and capital
markets—price the results.

The synthesis here draws on a recent stock-taking of the field [@morgan2018], on
the theories-in-use program for building organic marketing theory
[@zeithaml2019], and on a body of work that connects marketing organization,
market orientation, branding, channels, customer management, and human capital to
firm performance. Two commitments run through all of it. The first is
*integration*: a marketing strategy is a coherent pattern of decisions, not a
list of independent marketing-mix moves, and most of the field's empirical work
has paradoxically studied the parts rather than the pattern [@morgan2018]. The
second is *accountability*: strategy is judged by customer, financial,
stock-market, and societal outcomes, so the seminar repeatedly forces the
soft-sounding constructs of strategy—orientation, capability, culture,
relationships—into contact with hard outcome data.

By the end of the chapter a reader should be able to (i) state the formal
anatomy of marketing strategy and locate any given study within it, (ii)
distinguish theory-building from theory-testing research and run a
theories-in-use study competently, (iii) reason about *why* a firm organizes
marketing the way it does using the logic of governance and transaction costs,
and (iv) write down estimators—latent growth curves, panel models with
instruments, event studies—that turn strategic constructs into testable
parameters and say precisely what breaks their identification.

## The Anatomy of Marketing Strategy

A useful definition fixes the object before the analysis begins. The field's
modern consensus treats marketing strategy as an organization's integrated
pattern of decisions specifying its crucial choices about products, markets,
marketing activities, and marketing resources, in the service of offering value
to customers and achieving the organization's objectives.

> Marketing strategy is "an organization's integrated pattern of decisions that
> specify its crucial choices concerning products, markets, marketing activities
> and marketing resources in the creation, communication and/or delivery of
> products that offer value to customers in exchanges with the organization and
> thereby enables the organization to achieve specific objectives."

Two features of this definition do real work. First, it is about a *pattern* of
decisions, not a single decision; coherence across choices is constitutive of
strategy. Second, it is explicitly *means–ends*: choices are evaluated against
objectives, which makes performance the natural dependent variable.

@morgan2018 sharpen the definition by crossing two binary distinctions. The
first separates *what* a firm decides (strategy content) from *how* it makes and
realizes those decisions (strategy process). The second separates *formulation*
(figuring out what to do) from *implementation* (doing it). Crossing them yields
four sub-domains that exhaust the field and let any study be placed on a single
map (@fig-strategy-quadrants).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-strategy-quadrants
%%| fig-cap: "The four sub-domains of marketing strategy obtained by crossing formulation versus implementation with content versus process [@morgan2018]. Most empirical work clusters in the content row; process research, and integrated-program (versus single-tactic) research, remain comparatively thin."
flowchart TB
  subgraph FORM["Formulation — figuring out what to do"]
    FC["Formulation-Content<br/>Goals a strategy must deliver and the<br/>broad strategic decisions to achieve them<br/>(targets, value proposition, positioning)"]
    FP["Formulation-Process<br/>Mechanisms used to develop goals and<br/>select broad strategic means<br/>(timing, target, desired positioning)"]
  end
  subgraph IMPL["Implementation — doing it"]
    IC["Implementation-Content<br/>Detailed integrated marketing-program<br/>tactics, actions, and resource deployments"]
    IP["Implementation-Process<br/>Mechanisms to identify, select, and realize<br/>the tactics that deliver content decisions"]
  end
  FC -.->|content| IC
  FP -.->|process| IP
```

The taxonomy is not bookkeeping; it diagnoses where the field is thin. A review
of nineteen years of marketing-strategy research finds that most studies examine
*individual* marketing-mix instruments rather than integrated marketing programs,
so the very integration the definition foregrounds is under-studied
[@morgan2018]. The same review documents three further patterns that should
shape a doctoral reading list: roughly half of published studies are logic- or
data-driven rather than theory-driven, indicating a shortage of native theory;
papers increasingly assemble *multiple* borrowed theories rather than developing
or testing a single one; and qualitative method has dwindled toward zero. The
last point matters because theory-*building*—as opposed to theory-*testing*—often
needs exactly the qualitative tools the field has been abandoning, which is the
motivation for the next section.

## Building Native Theory: Theories-in-Use

Marketing's most-cited papers disproportionately advance native theory, yet the
field habitually borrows its theory wholesale from economics and psychology
[@zeithaml2019]. The *theories-in-use* (TIU) approach is a disciplined remedy:
it builds organic marketing theory from the mental models practitioners actually
use, rather than from constructs imported from other disciplines.

A theory-in-use is a person's mental model of how things work in a particular
context—a set of "if–then" relationships linking actions to outcomes
[@argyris1974theory; @zaltman1982theory]. The construct is defined against its
foil. *Espoused theories* are the mental models people claim or purport to hold;
a TIU is the model that actually governs behavior. The two can diverge sharply
because respondents often *have* a working model they cannot *articulate*, so a
method that merely records what informants say they believe will recover the
espoused theory and miss the operative one. TIU research is therefore grounded
simultaneously in the informant's mind and the researcher's, and is appropriate
when the goal is to construct organic theory, to extend or disambiguate existing
perspectives, or to guide subsequent empirical work [@zeithaml2019].

It helps to fix the relationship between TIU and the adjacent grounded-theory
family. Grounded theory is the broad methodological genus for inductively
building theory from data; case study and ethnography are sibling approaches
within it. TIU is best read as a focused species: it inherits grounded theory's
inductive, iterative coding discipline but trains it specifically on eliciting
the if–then causal maps that constitute informants' working theories.

@fig-tiu-process lays out the process as a pipeline from elicitation to a
publishable theory, with the iteration that is the method's signature.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-tiu-process
%%| fig-cap: "The theories-in-use research process: iterative elicitation and coding move from raw informant accounts to constructs, propositions, and a parsimonious theory [@zeithaml2019]. The dashed feedback edge marks the extensive iteration that distinguishes TIU from one-pass qualitative coding."
flowchart LR
  A["Elicit theories-in-use<br/>(in-depth interviews;<br/>active listening)"] --> B["Construct development<br/>via abstraction<br/>(open coding)"]
  B --> C["Proposition development<br/>(axial coding:<br/>link two or more concepts)"]
  C --> D["Argument development"]
  D --> E["Parsimonious theory<br/>(selective coding)"]
  E -.->|iterate / mosaic filling| A
```

The analytic core is a coding sequence. *Construct development* proceeds by
**abstraction**—identifying elements that are subsets of a broader, more abstract
element; elements that co-occur or covary; and elements that are neither nested
nor necessarily co-occurring and therefore demand separate constructs.
*Proposition development* proceeds by **axial coding**, linking two or more
concepts into testable if–then statements. *Argument development* assembles the
propositions into an explanation. The work then closes with **selective
coding**: choosing a parsimonious subset of propositions that carries the theory
without redundancy.

The craft surrounding the coding is what separates competent TIU work from
journalism. Skilled practice combines extensive iteration, active listening, and
*brief suspension*—deferring the researcher's own theory long enough to hear the
informant's—with depth over breadth, openness to new issues, appreciation of
conflict in informant accounts, *mosaic filling* (assembling a coherent picture
from partial accounts), explicit bias recognition, clear demarcation of the
study's limits, and disciplined paper-craft [@zeithaml2019]. The method's
boundaries are equally explicit: it is built for theory construction, not theory
testing, and informants' limited knowledge bounds what can be recovered, though
even uninformed respondents reliably surface their espoused theories. Promising
domains for the approach include reexamining an unquestioned assumption,
adjudicating conflicting firm-versus-customer viewpoints, and resolving conflict
among stakeholders, with open methodological questions about optimal sample
size, eliciting causal connections, and alternative probing techniques.

::: {.callout-note}
## Rigor in TIU research

Because TIU is interpretive, its credibility rests on demonstrated rigor rather
than on standard errors. Reviewers look for transparent elicitation protocols,
evidence of iteration to saturation, traceability from raw accounts through
construct and proposition coding, explicit treatment of disconfirming cases, and
candid demarcation of the study's limits [@zeithaml2019]. These criteria are the
qualitative analogue of identification assumptions: they specify the conditions
under which the inferred theory can be believed.
:::

## Marketing Excellence and the Marketing Organization

If TIU asks how to *build* theory about strategy, the marketing-organization
literature asks what *inside* the firm produces strategic success.
@moorman2016 define **marketing excellence** as "a superior ability to perform
essential customer-facing activities that improve customer, financial, stock
market, and societal outcomes." The definition is deliberately outcome-anchored:
excellence is not a posture but a measurable capacity whose payoff is observable
across four outcome classes.

Excellence rests on four elements of the marketing organization (MARORG) and is
expressed through seven activities. The four elements are *capabilities*—complex
bundles of firm-level skills and knowledge that perform marketing tasks and adapt
the firm to marketplace change; *configuration*—the organizational structures,
metrics, and incentive and control systems that shape marketing activity; *human
capital*—the people who create, implement, and evaluate strategy; and
*culture*—the shared values, beliefs, behaviors, and artifacts (stories, rituals)
that guide thinking and action throughout the firm [@moorman2016]. These four
elements are mobilized through seven activities, conveniently the "7 A's"
(@tbl-seven-as).

| Activity | What the firm does |
|---|---|
| **Anticipating** | Reads marketplace changes before they arrive |
| **Adapting** | Reshapes the firm to fit those changes |
| **Aligning** | Coordinates processes, structures, and people |
| **Activating** | Triggers efficient, effective individual and organizational behavior |
| **Accountability** | Creates responsibility for marketing performance |
| **Attracting** | Draws in financial, human, and other resources |
| **Asset management** | Develops and deploys marketing assets |

: The seven activities through which the marketing organization's four elements are mobilized into marketing excellence [@moorman2016]. {#tbl-seven-as}

The MARORG framework is a *capability* theory of strategy, and it inherits the
resource-based logic developed elsewhere in this book: a capability confers
sustained advantage when it is valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and embedded in
an organization able to exploit it. Capabilities of this kind are precisely what
event studies later price when they reward acquirers with strong marketing
capability [@germann2015].

### Market Orientation

The most influential operationalization of "customer-facing capability" is
**market orientation**, the implementation of the marketing concept. @kohli1990
define it as "the organizationwide generation of market intelligence pertaining
to current and future customer needs, dissemination of the intelligence across
departments, and responsiveness to it." The definition decomposes a culture into
three observable behaviors—intelligence *generation*, *dissemination*, and
*responsiveness*—and thereby makes an abstract orientation measurable
(@fig-market-orientation).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-market-orientation
%%| fig-cap: "Market orientation as three observable behaviors. Exogenous market factors and current and future customer needs feed intelligence generation; intelligence is disseminated across departments; the firm responds. Coordinated, cross-departmental work sustains the cycle, and profitability is a consequence rather than a component [@kohli1990]."
flowchart LR
  E["Exogenous market factors<br/>+ current & future customer needs"] --> G["Generation<br/>of market intelligence"]
  G --> D["Dissemination<br/>across departments"]
  D --> R["Responsiveness"]
  R --> P["Profitability<br/>(a consequence)"]
  R -.->|feedback| E
```

Three pillars underpin the construct. *Customer focus* construes market
intelligence broadly, spanning both the exogenous market factors that shape
customer needs and customers' current and future needs themselves. *Coordinated
marketing* requires one or more departments to work jointly toward a shared
understanding, so orientation is organization-wide rather than the property of a
marketing department. *Profitability* is deliberately placed as a *consequence*
of market orientation rather than a component of it—a modeling choice that keeps
the construct conceptually clean and lets profitability serve as a dependent
variable. A terminological note carries strategic weight: "market orientation"
is preferred to "marketing orientation" because it is less politically charged
inside the firm and keeps the focus on the market rather than on a single
function [@kohli1990].

## Branding as Strategic Asset

Branding is where marketing strategy is most fully expressed as a financial
asset, and a large literature now connects brand-related actions to capital-market
outcomes. @swaminathan2022 synthesize this brand–finance interface, building on
earlier reviews of how marketing creates shareholder value
[@srivastava1998; @keller2006; @edeling2016; @edeling2021] and assembling well
over a hundred studies that link brand actions to stock-market outcomes,
supplemented by a smaller set using accounting-based metrics. The chapter on
@sec-branding develops the behavioral and valuation machinery in full; the
present treatment isolates the *strategic* logic—how brand actions are
classified and how they reach firm value.

### Measuring the Financial Impact of Brands

Four measurement families dominate. *Event studies* read the market's valuation
of a discrete brand action from short-window stock returns. *Response models*
extend the logic to continuous, ongoing brand activity. A third family decomposes
risk into *idiosyncratic* and *systematic* components, since strong brands can
lower a firm's risk as well as raise its returns. The fourth uses **firm value**,
operationalized as Tobin's $q$—the ratio of a firm's market value to the
replacement cost of its assets,
$$
q = \frac{\text{market value of the firm}}{\text{replacement cost of assets}}.
$$ {#eq-tobins-q}
Values of $q$ above one indicate that markets price the firm above the cost of
rebuilding its tangible assets, the wedge being attributable to intangibles such
as brand. The measure has drawn methodological criticism [@bendle2018], to which
the literature has offered replies [@peters2017]. Empirically, a brand's
Tobin's $q$ moves with corporate branding strategy [@Rao_2004], with the
characteristics of the brand portfolio [@morgan2009], and with advertising
[@wang2008]. Accounting-based performance remains important for tracing the
*indirect* path from brand action to financial value.

### A Taxonomy of Brand Actions

@swaminathan2022 classify brand actions on two axes—*cause* and *scope*—that
together organize the empirical findings (@tbl-brand-actions). On cause, actions
are *proactive* (firm-initiated) or *reactive* (responses to external events such
as recalls or disputes). On scope, actions are *strategic* (broad, long-horizon:
targeting, segmentation, diversification, new-product introduction, rebranding,
brand architecture, acquisitions) or *tactical* (short-horizon marketing-mix
moves).

| | **Strategic** (broad, long-term) | **Tactical** (short-term) |
|---|---|---|
| **Proactive** | Brand introduction and innovation; brand architecture (house of brands vs. branded house); brand leverage; reputational capital, CSR, sociopolitical activism | Name changes; quality improvement; advertising; social-media and word-of-mouth communication; pricing and channels; celebrity endorsement |
| **Reactive** | (Strategic responses to crises and structural threats) | Product recalls; trademark disputes; brand crises (e.g., boycotts) |

: Brand actions classified by cause (proactive/reactive) and scope (strategic/tactical), with representative examples from the brand–finance literature [@swaminathan2022]. {#tbl-brand-actions}

A conceptual caution belongs here. Managers are paid to be proactive, but
proactivity is not unconditionally good. A *bias toward intervention*—what one
might call naive interventionism—favors actions that produce small, visible gains
while seeding the possibility of large, later harm, precisely because restraint
from action is rarely rewarded.[^taleb] Distinguishing value-creating proactivity
from intervention-for-its-own-sake is an open empirical question the taxonomy
helps frame.

[^taleb]: The asymmetry—visible small gains now against invisible large risks
later—is a general feature of intervention under uncertainty, and it cautions
against treating "proactive" as a synonym for "good" in brand strategy.

### How Brand Actions Reach Firm Value

Two theoretical perspectives explain *why* brand actions move financial outcomes.
Under **signaling theory**, brands are credible signals of quality to consumers
and investors alike, and the credibility of a signal depends on the signaler, the
signal's quality, the receiver, the signaling environment (increasingly social
media), and the feedback loop from receiver back to signaler [@connelly2010].
Under **resource-based theory**, a brand generates value when it is valuable,
rare, costly to imitate, and exploited by an organized firm—the same conditions
that make any resource a source of sustained competitive advantage. Between brand
action and firm value lie *mediators*—brand-quality perceptions, attitudes,
engagement (understudied), marketplace outcomes such as customer lifetime value
and market share, and organization- and industry-level processes such as barriers
to entry and analyst coverage—and *moderators*—advertising and other mix
variables, prior brand strength, marketing capabilities, and competitive
intensity.

The findings sort cleanly onto the taxonomy. Proactive-strategic actions—brand
introduction and innovation—are value-creating on revenue, profitability, and
firm value, and brand architecture choices trade off efficiency against risk: a
*branded house* (one master brand) yields efficiency and lower customization and
cannibalization but concentrates risk, relative to a *house of brands*
[@Rao_2004]. Proactive-tactical actions—name changes that signal strategic
redirection, quality improvements, advertising acting both directly (signaling
and spillover to investors) and indirectly (through brand meaning and strength),
social-media and word-of-mouth communication, pricing and distribution, and
celebrity endorsement—have effects that are generally positive but can cut both
ways. Reactive actions are sharpest: product recalls depress stock returns and
spill onto competitors, with prior reputation and advertising serving as a
double-edged sword—dampening *unintentional* harm but exacerbating *intentional*
harm such as corporate social irresponsibility; trademark disputes reward
plaintiffs almost regardless of verdict while punishing defendants on unfavorable
ones; and brand crises propagate through social media. Across all cells,
contingent factors—the number and strength of competitors, and the quality and
speed of brand actions—moderate the impact on customer-based brand equity. The
hyperconnected environment in which these signals now travel, and its
consequences for who owns brand meaning, is the subject of @swaminathan2020 and
is taken up in @sec-branding.

## Channels and Customer Management

Strategy must be *organized* and *delivered*, and the channels-and-customer
literature supplies the governance logic for both. Three threads matter for a
seminar: how firms choose organizational form for marketing tasks, how they
govern exchange with partners, and how relationships and customer engagement
evolve over time.

### The Temporary Marketing Organization

Much marketing work is done by *temporary* organizations—"temporally bounded
group[s] of interdependent actors formed to perform a complex task"
[@burke2016]—where "temporally bounded" means termination is institutionalized
from the outset [@hadida2018]. A pure **stand-alone** temporary organization has
a discrete time horizon and, unlike a joint venture or start-up, lacks both a
*history* of member interaction and a *future*. The absence of a shared past
induces information asymmetry about members' task ability, which invites
self-selection and signaling and requires explicit enforcement mechanisms that
are themselves hard to craft given the form's discreteness.

The form a temporary organization takes depends on whether it can borrow a past
or a future from its context. It can do so through members' prior relationships
(yielding a **hybrid** form) or by embedding within a permanent organization
(yielding a **fully embedded** form). Borrowing is not free: strong prior ties
can constrain information access [@granovetter1973] even as they supply quality
control and reduce principal–agent divergence. Three drivers—*task*, *time*, and
*team*—select the form (@fig-temporary-org). Greater task novelty raises the need
for organization-specific selection and enforcement and favors the stand-alone
form; shorter task duration lowers the feasibility of crafting bespoke mechanisms
and favors the hybrid form; greater team heterogeneity raises the need for
enforcement through low-powered incentives and favors the fully embedded form
[@hadida2018].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-temporary-org
%%| fig-cap: "Drivers of temporary-marketing-organization form. Task novelty, task duration, and team heterogeneity jointly determine whether selection and enforcement needs are met internally (stand-alone), borrowed from prior relationships (hybrid), or supplied by a permanent host (fully embedded) [@hadida2018]."
flowchart TB
  T1["Task novelty (high)"] --> SA["Stand-alone<br/>(organization-specific<br/>selection + enforcement)"]
  T2["Task duration (short)"] --> HY["Hybrid<br/>(selection/enforcement<br/>borrowed from prior ties)"]
  T3["Team heterogeneity (high)"] --> FE["Fully embedded<br/>(enforcement via<br/>low-powered incentives)"]
```

The mechanism connecting form to performance runs through *portability*: the
selection and enforcement benefits of context can be portable or supplied
exogenously, from preexisting agent relationships (hybrid) or from a permanent
organization's features (fully embedded) [@hadida2018]. Portability is uneven.
Greater task novelty *lowers* the portability of a hybrid's selection benefits,
raising the need for organization-specific selection, whereas a hybrid's
enforcement benefits remain portable regardless of task. A fully embedded
organization's selection and enforcement benefits are *less* portable than a
hybrid's. Two performance outcomes follow from matching form to task. Output
*creativity*, which is tied to selection, is greatest when the novelty of the
task matches the selection effort; decision-making *speed*, which is tied to
enforcement, is greatest when novelty matches enforcement effort—but
*over*-organizing enforcement backfires, lowering speed through reactance and
diminished intrinsic motivation. For the manager, task novelty, time pressure,
and team heterogeneity are the inputs that should determine organizational form.

### Governing Exchange: Transaction Cost Analysis

When the firm must decide whether to make, buy, or ally, **transaction cost
analysis** (TCA) supplies the governance logic. TCA sits within the New
Institutional Economics that supplanted neoclassical treatments of the firm, and
it views the firm itself as a *governance structure* rather than a production
function [@rindfleisch1997]. Its appeal in marketing is twofold: it centers on
*exchange*, the discipline's native unit, and its constructs are amenable to
survey measurement.

TCA rests on a compact set of assumptions, organized into behavioral assumptions
about actors and dimensions that describe the transaction (@tbl-tca).

| Behavioral assumptions | Transactional dimensions |
|---|---|
| Bounded rationality | Environmental uncertainty |
| Opportunism | Asset specificity |
| Risk neutrality | Transaction frequency |

: The behavioral assumptions and transactional dimensions of transaction cost analysis [@rindfleisch1997]. {#tbl-tca}

The governance logic is a cost comparison. When the costs of adaptability,
performance evaluation, and safeguarding are absent or minimal, actors choose
*market* governance; when the expense of internal organization is exceeded by the
production-cost benefits of bringing the transaction inside, the firm
*integrates*. The decisive driver is **asset specificity**: investments specialized
to a particular exchange create quasi-rents that opportunistic partners can
expropriate under bounded rationality, so high specificity, especially when
compounded by environmental uncertainty, pushes governance toward hierarchy. The
framework applies to vertical integration, to vertical inter-organizational
relationships, and to horizontal ones [@rindfleisch1997]. As an identification
matter, the empirical challenge is that governance form is *chosen*: firms select
into integration on the basis of specificity and uncertainty that the analyst
observes only partially, so naive regressions of performance on governance form
confound the treatment with its selection. Credible designs either model the
selection explicitly or exploit exogenous shifts in the cost of an asset's
specificity.

### Relationship Dynamics: Commitment Velocity

Relationships between exchange partners are not static, and treating them as such
discards the information in their *trajectories*. @palmatier2013 introduce
**commitment velocity**—the rate and direction of change in commitment—and argue
that the dynamic elements of relational constructs forecast future behavior and
performance better than their static levels. The program rests on three tenets:
exchange performance reflects both static and dynamic elements of relational
constructs, with the dynamic elements more predictive; the growth trajectories of
trust, commitment, and relational norms are distinctive and path-dependent,
shaped by construct-specific time-varying processes; and as relationships age,
both the links among relational constructs and their relative weights in
determining exchange outcomes themselves change.

The estimator is a **latent growth curve model** (LGCM). For dyad $i$ observed at
time $t$, a relational construct $y_{it}$ (say commitment) is decomposed into an
individual-specific intercept (level) and slope (velocity),
$$
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i\, t + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_i \\ \beta_i\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}\mu_\alpha \\ \mu_\beta\end{pmatrix}
+ \begin{pmatrix}\zeta_{\alpha i} \\ \zeta_{\beta i}\end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-lgcm}
where $\alpha_i$ is the dyad's baseline commitment, $\beta_i$ its commitment
velocity, $\mu_\alpha$ and $\mu_\beta$ the population means, and the random
effects $(\zeta_{\alpha i}, \zeta_{\beta i})$ capture heterogeneity across dyads
with $\varepsilon_{it}$ the time-specific disturbance. Identification of the
slope factor requires at least three waves of panel data and rests on the usual
LGCM assumptions: a correctly specified (here linear) growth form, errors
uncorrelated with the latent factors, and—when velocity is used to predict
performance—no time-varying confounder driving both commitment growth and the
outcome. Estimated on six years of longitudinal data, commitment velocity
predicts performance; in a matched, multi-source study of its antecedents,
customer trust and dynamic capabilities raise velocity early in a relationship
while investment capabilities matter more as the relationship matures
[@palmatier2013]. The substantive lesson—that *change* in a relational construct
carries information beyond its *level*—generalizes to any longitudinally measured
strategic construct.

### Customer Engagement Marketing

The frontier of customer management treats customers as quasi-employees who
perform marketing functions. **Customer engagement marketing** is "a firm's
deliberate effort to motivate, empower, and measure customer contributions to
marketing functions" [@harmeling2016]. The construct is distinguished from
ordinary relationship marketing by its target: it elicits customer *behaviors*
that contribute to the firm's marketing—referrals, content creation, peer
help—rather than merely transactions. Two psychological mechanisms drive these
contributions. Firms deploy **experiential** engagement initiatives, which
immerse customers in events and experiences, and **ownership** engagement
initiatives, which grant customers psychological ownership of the brand or its
outcomes; both raise customers' motivation and ability to contribute, with the
firm's role being to motivate, empower, and then *measure* the resulting
contributions [@harmeling2016]. The accountability emphasis—measuring
contributions—returns the construct to the outcome-anchored definition of
marketing excellence with which the seminar began.

## Human Capital: The CMO and Firm Performance

The marketing-organization framework names human capital as one of its four
elements; the cleanest test of its strategic value asks whether the senior
marketing role pays off in firm performance. The natural unit of analysis is the
presence of a **chief marketing officer** (CMO) in the top management team
[@nath2008], and the sharpest estimate of its value comes from a study finding
that firms with a CMO exhibit roughly **15% higher Tobin's $q$** than firms
without one [@germann2015].

That headline number is interesting only if it is *causal*, and the design is
built to make it credible. CMO presence is not randomly assigned: firms that
appoint a CMO may differ systematically—in their reliance on marketing, their
governance, their growth prospects—from firms that do not, so a cross-sectional
comparison of performance confounds the CMO effect with whatever drives the
appointment. @germann2015 address this with two complementary strategies. First,
**panel data** with firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity, so
identification comes from *within-firm* changes in CMO presence rather than from
comparing different firms. The fixed-effects estimand is
$$
y_{it} = \gamma\, \text{CMO}_{it} + \mathbf{x}_{it}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
        + \mu_i + \tau_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-cmo-fe}
where $y_{it}$ is firm performance (Tobin's $q$), $\text{CMO}_{it}$ indicates CMO
presence, $\mu_i$ is a firm fixed effect, $\tau_t$ a year effect, and $\gamma$
the parameter of interest. Fixed effects do not, however, defeat *time-varying*
endogeneity—reverse causality (rising performance funds a CMO appointment) or a
contemporaneous shock driving both. The second strategy therefore adds
**instrumental variables**: a valid instrument shifts the probability of CMO
presence (relevance) without affecting firm performance except through the CMO
(the exclusion restriction). The exclusion restriction is the assumption that
*cannot* be tested from data and on which the causal claim ultimately rests; it
is where identification breaks if the instrument has an independent path to
performance. Relative to the original CMO-presence study [@nath2008], the design
extends the time horizon, broadens the set of industries, and adds the panel and
instrumental-variable machinery [@germann2015]—a worked illustration of the
seminar's recurring point that a strategic construct becomes a *finding* only
when its estimator and its identifying assumptions are stated in full.

## Key Takeaways

- Marketing strategy is an *integrated pattern* of decisions evaluated against
  objectives; @morgan2018's content/process × formulation/implementation grid
  (@fig-strategy-quadrants) locates any study and reveals the field's bias toward
  single tactics over integrated programs.
- **Theories-in-use** builds native marketing theory from practitioners' working
  if–then models through iterative abstraction and axial, then selective, coding;
  it is a theory-*building*, not theory-*testing*, method [@zeithaml2019].
- **Marketing excellence** is an outcome-anchored capability resting on four
  organizational elements (capabilities, configuration, human capital, culture)
  mobilized through seven activities [@moorman2016]; **market orientation**
  operationalizes the customer-facing capability as intelligence generation,
  dissemination, and responsiveness [@kohli1990].
- Brand actions reach firm value through signaling and resource-based paths and
  are priced by markets; the cause × scope taxonomy organizes the evidence, and
  Tobin's $q$ (@eq-tobins-q) is the workhorse outcome [@swaminathan2022].
- Organizational form (the temporary marketing organization), governance
  (transaction cost analysis), relationship *dynamics* (commitment velocity,
  @eq-lgcm), and human capital (the CMO effect, @eq-cmo-fe) each become testable
  only once their estimator and identifying assumptions—selection, exclusion,
  correct growth form—are made explicit.
